items.title: Recap: training as minimising a loss over parameters
items.text: Training is reframed as minimising the loss L(θ) as a function of the parameters θ, with the data held fixed. Linear regression admits a closed-form solution via the normal equations, but its O(d³) cost and the absence of any closed form for neural networks motivate an iterative method that walks downhill on the loss landscape.
keyPoints: The loss is treated as a function of the parameters, not the data.
Closed-form least squares needs a d×d matrix inverse (about d³ work) and does not exist for neural networks.
Linear-regression loss is a convex bowl; neural-network losses have local minima, plateaus and saddle points.

evidence.quote: Think of it as a function of theta.
for a neural network there is no closed form at all

items.title: Gradient descent and the learning rate
items.text: Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the gradient: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ). The learning rate η is a hand-chosen hyperparameter. On L(w) = w² starting from w = 1, η = 0.1 converges smoothly, η = 0.9 oscillates but converges, and η = 1.1 diverges; a very small η converges slowly and can stall on plateaus.
keyPoints: Too large a learning rate overshoots and diverges (loss becomes NaN); too small is slow.
Choose η by sweeping a log scale and keeping the largest value that still decreases the loss steadily.

evidence.quote: theta new equals theta old minus eta times the gradient of L evaluated at theta old
the loss blows up to infinity

unsupportedSentences: On L(w) = w² starting from w = 1, η = 0.1 converges smoothly, η = 0.9 oscillates but converges, and η = 1.1 diverges; a very small η converges slowly and can stall on plateaus.

items.title: Stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent
items.text: Stochastic gradient descent replaces the full-batch gradient with the gradient of a random example, which is noisy but unbiased. Mini-batches of 32–512 examples reduce variance and parallelise well on GPUs. An epoch is one pass over the data; shuffling every epoch avoids biased batches, and decaying the learning rate lets SGD settle near a minimum.
keyPoints: The single-example gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full-batch gradient.
Iteration = one mini-batch update; epoch = one full pass (50,000 examples / batch 100 = 500 iterations).
SGD noise helps escape saddle points; a decaying learning rate lets the iterates settle.

evidence.quote: That estimate is noisy, but it's unbiased.
One epoch is one full pass over the training set.

unsupportedSentences: Mini-batches of 32–512 examples reduce variance and parallelise well on GPUs.

items.title: Chain rule and computational graphs
items.text: Backpropagation is an efficient application of the chain rule over a computational graph, not a new learning algorithm. The forward pass stores intermediate values; the backward pass multiplies each node's upstream gradient by its local derivative. Add gates distribute, multiply gates swap, max gates route, and gradients from multiple branches are summed.
keyPoints: Worked example f = (x + y)·z at x = −2, y = 5, z = −4 gives ∂f/∂x = ∂f/∂y = −4 and ∂f/∂z = 3.
Each node needs only its upstream gradient and its local derivative.
The backward pass costs about the same as one or two forward passes.

evidence.quote: It is just an efficient way of computing gradients
An add gate distributes the upstream gradient unchanged to all its inputs.

unsupportedSentences: Add gates distribute, multiply gates swap, max gates route, and gradients from multiple branches are summed.

items.title: Backpropagation through a two-layer network
items.text: For a two-layer sigmoid network with squared error, the output error δ₂ = ŷ − y gives ∂L/∂W₂ = δ₂hᵀ; propagating back through the sigmoid gives δ₁ = (W₂ᵀδ₂) ⊙ h(1 − h) and ∂L/∂W₁ = δ₁xᵀ. Because the sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25, deep sigmoid stacks suffer vanishing gradients. Gradient checking with centred differences validates an implementation.
keyPoints: Every weight gradient is the layer's error times the layer's input (transposed).
Sigmoid derivative h(1 − h) ≤ 0.25, so gradients shrink through many layers; ReLU avoids this.
Gradient check: relative error around 1e-7 indicates a correct implementation.

evidence.quote: delta one equals W two transpose delta two, times h times one minus h
h times one minus h is at most one quarter
